name: Poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra)

lead: Sculptra is a Galderma injectable of poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), used to restore cheek and midface volume, soften cheek lines and rebuild a gaunt face after weight loss. Results build gradually over weeks, giving fuller cheeks, softer folds and better-defined contours.

Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, which add volume immediately, PLLA microparticles prompt a mild inflammatory response that leads the body to lay down its own collagen. The FDA first approved it in 2004 for facial fat loss in people with HIV, and later for nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report better skin elasticity, wrinkle reduction and facial volume, with effects sustained up to about 25 months.

paras: It is injected by trained clinicians, typically over several sessions spaced weeks apart, with volume building between visits. Looksmax forum discussion is limited to a few questions about regaining volume in a gaunt face after weight loss.

Reported adverse events are mostly mild to moderate: bruising, hematoma, tenderness, swelling and nodules. A 2026 systematic review reported at least one serious case. Lumps are linked to technique and product selection, which is why it is administered by clinicians.

chain: Fuller cheeks, softer folds, defined contours
angle.text: Sculptra is injected to bring volume back to the cheeks and midface, softening cheek lines and rebuilding a gaunt face after weight loss. PLLA triggers the body's own collagen production, so the result builds over weeks, and randomized trials report effects lasting up to about two years.

lead: Sculptra is a brand of injectable poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a synthetic, biocompatible and biodegradable polymer, marketed by Galderma as a collagen-stimulating dermal treatment [1][2]. It is used to restore volume in the cheeks and midface, to soften nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles, and, in its original indication, to correct facial lipoatrophy in HIV [1][3][4]. Clinicians also use it off-label on other areas, including the buttocks, hands and neck [4][5].

Unlike conventional hyaluronic acid fillers, PLLA is described as a biostimulator: its microparticles are said to provoke a controlled subclinical inflammatory response that lays down collagen, so results emerge over weeks to months and typically involve several treatment sessions [2][1]. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report improvements in skin quality, volume and lipoatrophy scores, with benefits sustained up to 25 months, and adverse events that are mostly mild to moderate [3].

In looksmaxxing communities, it is discussed mainly as an option for a gaunt face after weight loss; the community material is limited to a few forum questions [6]. A registered study of PLLA in people using GLP-1 weight-loss drugs reflects a wider clinical interest in treating the facial volume loss that can accompany rapid weight loss [7].
infobox: 3 August 2004, facial lipoatrophy in HIV (FDA PMA P030050)
Nasolabial folds (2009) and cheek wrinkles (2023), per Grokipedia [1]

paras: PLLA is a polymer of L-lactic acid. Grokipedia describes it as degrading by hydrolysis into lactic acid over roughly 6 to 24 months and being metabolised, with solid irregular particles in the 40 to 63 micron range [1]. A 2018 review states that the size and chemistry of the microparticles are central to the subclinical inflammatory response that stimulates collagen deposition and that this differentiates PLLA from other treatments [2]. Wikipedia's article on polylactic acid says PLA degrades into lactic acid and is used in absorbable sutures, screws and plates, and describes Sculptra as an injectable filler that appears to work through a foreign-body reaction in which macrophages release signals such as TGF-beta that prompt fibroblasts to make collagen.

Because it works by biostimulation, treatment typically involves several sessions spaced weeks apart, followed by maintenance, according to Grokipedia [1]. Wikipedia says collagen takes roughly one to one and a half months to form after injection, that bruising and swelling usually settle within about a week, and that patients are told to massage the treated area afterwards to help it stay smooth [4]. A 2022 review by Christen describes response as varying between patients and recommends several sessions so collagen stimulation can unfold and overcorrection is avoided [5]. The wiki does not reproduce preparation or injection technique.

In the face, PLLA is used for midface and cheek volume, nasolabial folds, cheek wrinkles and contour defects, and trials have also looked at temple volume loss and acne scars [3][8][9][10][11]. People describe the aim as replacing the fullness lost with age or weight loss so cheeks and temples look less hollow [6].

Off-label body use includes a non-surgical buttock augmentation, sometimes called a Sculptra butt lift, as well as hands, neck and chest, according to Grokipedia and Wikipedia [1][4]. A 2025 international consensus statement addresses injectable PLLA for body aesthetic treatments [12], and the Christen 2022 review of body applications found that the literature is mostly case series and retrospective studies with few randomized placebo-controlled trials [5]. A registered chart review of Sculptra in non-facial skin conditions enrolled 498 people, and a small trial has examined cellulite of the buttocks and thighs [13][14].

The original FDA indication was restoration or correction of the signs of facial fat loss in people with HIV, where antiretroviral-related lipoatrophy hollows the cheeks [4]. That approval was based on small studies in people with HIV, and the FDA later approved non-HIV cosmetic uses even though complications had been reported to the agency, according to Wikipedia [4].

Systematic reviews. A 2024 systematic review in Polymers included 11 randomized trials in adults with facial aging or lipoatrophy; four showed increased dermal thickness and improved lipoatrophy and aesthetic scores, with effects sustained for at least 25 months, two showed superiority over injectable human collagen, and three favoured PLLA over a hyaluronic gel for lipoatrophy severity, skin quality, elasticity and satisfaction [3]. A 2026 systematic review of 14 studies of PLLA and calcium hydroxylapatite found improvements in elasticity, wrinkles and facial volume, with PLLA effects lasting up to 25 months versus 12 to 18 months for calcium hydroxylapatite.

Individual randomized trials. A randomized trial of Sculptra for cheek wrinkles compared it with no treatment in adults over 21 with moderate or severe wrinkles [8]. A split-face, double-blind non-inferiority trial compared a new PLLA filler (Gana V) with Sculptra in nasolabial folds [15]. A 2025 multicenter, evaluator-blinded superiority trial studied PLLA for midfacial volume loss and contour defects [9]. Randomized trials have also tested PLLA with microneedling radiofrequency for skin laxity and with fractional CO2 laser for acne scars [16][10]. A gene-expression analysis in a randomized comparison reported that PLLA triggered regeneration-related activity while calcium hydroxylapatite induced inflammation-related activity [17].

Histology. Christen's review cites a study of 14 people given PLLA behind the ear in which biopsies showed increased type I collagen at 3 and 6 months [5]. Registered studies are examining histological changes in women at different menopausal stages and skin changes by non-invasive imaging [18][19].

Registered studies. Trials of Sculptra for midface volume deficit (205 participants) and nasolabial folds (80 participants) are registered as completed [20][21]. Smaller studies cover temple volume loss and cellulite [11][14]. A phase 2 study of PLLA in people using GLP-1 drugs, who may experience facial laxity, is registered but not yet recruiting [7].

Limits. The 2026 reviewers assessed risk of bias with the ROB2 tool, and a 2024 review notes that studies vary in design and comparators [3]. Christen's review concludes that larger standardized studies are needed for body applications [5].

Across randomized trials the main adverse events were bruising, hematoma, tenderness, nodules and edema, all mild to moderate in intensity [3]. The 2026 systematic review lists pain and swelling at the injection site as the most frequent effects and describes at least one serious case. Christen's review calls the safety profile good, with mostly minor transient events, and identifies nodules as the main concern, linking early nodule formation to preparation and dilution factors in body studies [5].

Grokipedia states contraindications include hypersensitivity to components, active skin infection, pregnancy, breastfeeding and a history of keloid scarring, and says rare complications include delayed nodules and granulomas, vascular occlusion with a reported retinal artery occlusion case, and infection [1]. It also says that, unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, PLLA cannot be dissolved with hyaluronidase [1]. Wikipedia's dermal filler article describes embolization into eye arteries causing blindness as a recognised risk of fillers in general.

PLLA microparticles are described as promoting a subclinical inflammatory response that leads to collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix, so volume is restored gradually rather than immediately [2]. Grokipedia says injected microspheres trigger a controlled foreign-body reaction leading to new type I and III collagen over several months, with visible improvement from about 4 to 6 weeks and full effects at 3 to 6 months, and notes that deep injection can give some immediate lift [1].

Wikipedia says PLLA first appeared in medicine in sutures and implants. Grokipedia dates PLLA's medical use to the 1970s and says it was first sold in Europe as New-Fill, with CE mark certification in 1999 [1].

According to the FDA's premarket approval record (P030050), the application was received on 1 December 2003 and decided on 3 August 2004, with the original indication being restoration or correction of facial fat loss in people with HIV; the record lists 54 later supplements and names Q-Med AB as applicant on the current page. Wikipedia describes the US marketer at the time as Dermik Laboratories, the American arm of Aventis Dermatology [4]. Grokipedia says the FDA extended labelling to nasolabial folds in 2009 and added cheek wrinkles in April 2023, and that ownership passed from Sanofi-Aventis (Dermik) to Valeant in 2011 and to Galderma in 2014 [1].

Galderma, which lists Sculptra among its main aesthetics brands alongside Restylane and Dysport, was formed by L'Oreal and Nestle in 1981, acquired the Swedish device maker Q-Med in 2010, was sold by Nestle in 2019 to a consortium led by EQT, and listed on the Swiss exchange in March 2024.

In the US, dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices and must be injected by or under a licensed provider; Sculptra was approved through the FDA premarket approval route. In the UK and EEA, fillers are regulated as devices with a CE mark that covers production standards rather than proven efficacy.

The community material is a single looksmax.org thread in which a user with a gaunt face when losing weight asks for opinions on Sculptra, planning treatment within weeks [6]. Adjacent discussion concerns weight-loss face changes, where clinical interest is reflected in a registered trial of PLLA for laxity in GLP-1 users [7]. Grokipedia advises against using PLLA in the lips or under the eyes [1].

Registered studies include a trial of combination treatment with a Sofwave ultrasound device, studies of imaging and histological changes after biostimulator treatment, and the GLP-1 study [7][18][19][22]. Reviews of body applications call for larger standardized trials [5].

lore.intro: Community discussion of Sculptra is sparse; the main thread concerns using it for a hollow face after weight loss [6].
